intro: The CAGR Calculator finds the Compound Annual Growth Rate — the steady yearly rate at which an investment, business, or any value grew from a starting amount to an ending amount.
uses: It is used to compare investments held for different lengths of time, to judge a fund or stock by its annualised growth rather than its total gain, and to measure how fast a business metric such as revenue has grown.
formula: CAGR = (Ending Value ÷ Starting Value)^(1 ÷ Number of Years) − 1, shown as a percentage. Absolute return = (Ending Value − Starting Value) ÷ Starting Value × 100. Total gain = Ending Value − Starting Value.
example: Inputs: Starting Value = ₹50,000, Ending Value = ₹1,20,000, Number of Years = 5. Step 1: ratio = 1,20,000 ÷ 50,000 = 2.4. Step 2: CAGR = 2.4^(1 ÷ 5) − 1 = 2.4^0.2 − 1 = 0.1914, or 19.14% per year. Step 3: total gain = 1,20,000 − 50,000 = ₹70,000. Step 4: absolute return = 70,000 ÷ 50,000 × 100 = 140%.
howTo: Step 1: Enter the value at the start of the period in the "Starting Value (₹)" field.
Step 2: Enter the value at the end of the period in the "Ending Value (₹)" field.
Step 3: Enter the length of the period in the "Number of Years" field.
Step 4: Tap Calculate to see the CAGR, the absolute return, the total gain, and the period.
tips: CAGR smooths out the ups and downs — it shows the steady rate that would produce the same result, not the actual return in any single year.
Use CAGR to compare two investments held for different periods; total return alone is misleading when the periods differ.
A high CAGR over a short period is less meaningful than a steady CAGR over many years.
CAGR only needs the start value, end value, and time — it ignores any money added or withdrawn in between, so use it only when there were no extra deposits.
mistakes: Comparing total returns instead of CAGR when the holding periods are different.
Treating CAGR as the return earned every year — real yearly returns vary around it.
Using CAGR when money was added or withdrawn during the period, which makes the result wrong.
Entering the number of years as months, which makes the CAGR far too low.

faqs.a: CAGR is the Compound Annual Growth Rate — the constant yearly growth rate that would take a starting value to an ending value over a given number of years. For example, ₹50,000 growing to ₹1,20,000 in 5 years is a CAGR of 19.14%.

faqs.q: What is the difference between CAGR and absolute return?
faqs.a: Absolute return is the total gain as a percentage of the starting value, without considering time — 140% in the example above. CAGR spreads that growth over the years, giving 19.14% per year over 5 years.

faqs.q: Is a higher CAGR always better?
faqs.a: Not always. A higher CAGR is better for the same period and the same risk, but a very high CAGR over one year may come with high risk or luck. Compare CAGR over similar periods and consider the risk taken.
